title: Regulatory judgement - Silvering Homes Ltd (March 2026)
author: P007
summary: The Regulator of Social Housing's published judgement following the March 2026 inspection: Governance G1, Viability V2, Consumer C2, with damp and mould and complaint handling identified as areas for improvement.

blocks.p: *Copy of the judgement as published by the Regulator of Social Housing on 25 March 2026. Filed by the Governance team for reference.*
We have concluded that there are some weaknesses in Silvering Homes Ltd (Silvering) delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and improvement is needed.

Silvering has assurance that it is meeting its statutory health and safety responsibilities in relation to gas, electrical, fire, water and lift safety, and asbestos, with compliance above 98% in each area at the time of inspection. It has a recent stock condition survey for most of its homes and understands the condition of its stock. It engages well with tenants through its Customer Insight Group and tenants we spoke to described staff as approachable.

However, we found weaknesses in how Silvering identifies and responds to damp and mould. Investigations were not always carried out promptly; tenants were not consistently told what had been found and what would happen next; and there was limited follow-up to confirm that works had been effective. A disproportionate number of cases were concentrated on one estate, where repeat reports were common. Silvering has identified these issues and has a plan to address them, which it is at an early stage of implementing.

We also found weaknesses in complaint handling. Silvering's performance in responding to stage 1 complaints within the timescales of the Housing Ombudsman's Complaint Handling Code was inconsistent during 2025, and tenant satisfaction with complaint handling, as reported in its Tenant Satisfaction Measures, is low. Learning from complaints was not systematically captured or reported to the board.

Silvering has an accurate understanding of the diverse needs of its tenants and collects data on vulnerability, although this is not yet used consistently to prioritise repairs and damp and mould responses.

Our judgement that Silvering meets our governance requirements is based on evidence from the inspection. The board provides effective oversight and challenge, has a clear understanding of the areas where improvement is needed, and responded openly to our findings. Silvering has an effective risk management framework and an appropriate internal controls assurance framework. Silvering has adopted the NHF Code of Governance 2020 and reports that it complies with it.

Silvering meets our viability requirements and has the financial capacity to deal with a reasonable range of adverse scenarios, but needs to manage material financial risks to ensure continued compliance. Silvering's interest cover has fallen due to increased expenditure on its existing homes, including damp and mould remediation and building safety works, and higher interest costs. Its business plan relies on the successful delivery of efficiencies and on sales receipts from shared ownership. The board will need to continue to monitor headroom against its covenants closely while it delivers its investment programme.

We will continue to engage with Silvering through our routine stability check and regulatory engagement to seek assurance on the delivery of its improvement plans for damp and mould and complaint handling.

blocks.p: This has been a difficult summer for our repairs service. Routine repairs performance fell sharply from June, mainly because two electrician posts and a plasterer post have been vacant since the spring, colleagues took summer leave and we relied more on our overflow contractor Brightline Electrical, whose performance has been mixed. Emergency repairs have stayed strong. Daniel Kerr and Kwame Asante have a recovery plan, but I do not expect us to be back above 85% before the new year.

On damp and mould, the Awaab's Law processes introduced in April are working for most cases, but we are still seeing breaches of the timescales, mostly in the written summary step and mostly at Brenchley Gardens. I have asked Gareth Price to bring a deep-dive on breaches to the Chair by the end of October.

Orchard Fields phase 1 hands over on 2 October. Our first residents will move in the following week. The defects list from Castlemere is longer than we would like and we will not let homes until they are right.

Finally, I am asking the Board to approve a small, tightly controlled Microsoft 365 Copilot pilot (item 8). Done well, it could give our staff back time to spend with residents. Done badly, it could expose vulnerability data. The paper sets out how we will manage that risk.

title: Board Minutes - 24 September 2026
author: P039
summary: Draft minutes of the 24 September 2026 Board, including approval of the Copilot pilot, challenge on repairs and damp performance and the action for a damp breach deep-dive by 31 October.

kv: Kingsgate House, Board Room, and Microsoft Teams

blocks.p: Hilary Brandwood (Chair), Graham Sutcliffe (Vice Chair; Chair of Treasury & Finance), Dr Anita Rowe (Chair of Audit & Assurance), Marcia Thompson (resident board member; Chair of Customer Experience; Member Responsible for Complaints), Peter Okonjo, Helen Fairweather, Catherine Ellwood (Chief Executive).
**In attendance:** Martin Okafor, Rachel Dunmore, Gareth Price, Simone Achterberg, Joanne Pike (Company Secretary), Tom Lyle (item 7), Craig Whitmore (item 8).
Chris Dabrowski.
None.
Approved as a correct record. All matters arising were complete or on the agenda.

The Chair said the Board needed assurance, not reassurance, on damp and mould. It was not enough to know the processes existed; the Board needed to understand why breaches were still happening, who was affected and whether vulnerable households were being prioritised. Catherine Ellwood agreed and confirmed that Gareth Price would provide a deep-dive on Awaab's Law breaches to the Chair by 31 October, for circulation to the whole Board.

Graham Sutcliffe asked how much of the repairs decline was due to vacancies and how much to the overflow contractor. Gareth Price said both, roughly equally, and that Brightline's invoices often lacked job numbers which made reconciliation slow. Peter Okonjo asked whether the market supplement for electricians was large enough. Simone Achterberg said the posts would be re-advertised with an increased supplement in October.

Marcia Thompson challenged the statement that action A06 was complete, noting that the complaint figures in the pack showed stage 1 responses below 100% in June and July. Rachel Dunmore said the action had been marked complete because the resources and template were now in place; the outcome would be monitored at CEC. Marcia said she would rather the action stayed open until the outcome was achieved. **It was agreed that the Customer Experience Committee would review A06 in October.**

Dr Anita Rowe asked for a date by which the Rosemount Tower fire door actions would close. Gareth Price said the end of November. The Board noted the lift contractor's performance and asked for an update in November.

Tom Lyle reported that practical completion was on track for 2 October. Helen Fairweather asked about the cost of homes standing empty. Tom said the void rent loss would be included in the November development report. The Board asked that no home be let until signed off by Silvering's own team.

Craig Whitmore summarised the permissions work. Dr Rowe asked what would happen if a pilot user saw vulnerability data they should not. Simone Achterberg explained the near-miss reporting process in the draft policy. **Resolved: the Board approved the Copilot pilot for 30 users from 19 October 2026, subject to the three conditions in the paper being confirmed by the Chief Executive.**
Dr Rowe reported that the internal audit of damp and mould case management had given limited assurance; the full report would go to the Audit & Assurance Committee in October.

messages.body:
Catherine,

I was expecting Gareth's deep-dive on Awaab's Law breaches by 31 October, as we agreed at the September board (BA-26/31). I haven't seen it, and nobody has told me it would be late.

I am not looking for a polished paper. I need to understand three things before the board on the 26th: how many breaches there have been since the law came in and at which step; how many involved households with a vulnerability or children; and what is different now that means they won't happen again.

I'd also like to know whether the figures will reconcile with FieldLoop, given what internal audit said in October.

Can we speak this week?

Hilary

Hilary,

You're right, and I'm sorry - we should have told you before the deadline passed. That's on me.

We discussed it at the Exec this morning. Gareth will bring the full deep-dive to the board on 26 November, reconciled to FieldLoop by Kwame Asante as internal audit recommended. In the meantime Gareth will send you an interim note by Friday 6 November with the headline numbers you asked for.

I have asked Tessa to put 30 minutes in our diaries on Thursday.

Catherine

Hilary,

Ahead of Friday's note, the headline from FieldLoop as of today: {{fact:damp_cases_awaab}} cases have fallen under Awaab's Law, and {{fact:damp_breaches}} of them breached at least one timescale. Most breaches were at the written summary step, followed by late investigations. We currently have {{fact:damp_open}} open damp and mould cases.

The vulnerability breakdown is the part I want to check properly before I put it in writing, because the flag sits in Keystone rather than FieldLoop (internal audit finding 2).

The main changes since the summer: a mandatory summary template with an automatic alert, a second surveyor covering Brenchley Gardens two days a week, and a daily huddle between the planners and the damp team.

Gareth
